citation.authors: UK AI Security Institute (and Meridian Labs contributors)
citation.title: Inspect AI documentation: Sandboxing; Standard Tools; Custom Tools; Setting Limits; Multiple Scorers (Sandbox Access); Agent Bridge; Extensions; Sandbox extension API; inspect_ai.tool / inspect_ai.util reference

claims.planned: Sandbox environments are how Inspect runs model-generated code/tool calls in isolation; built-in providers: 'local' (no isolation) and 'docker'; others via extensions (k8s, proxmox, podman, modal, daytona etc. — list what docs list today)
claims.finding: Confirmed, with a nuance worth teaching: tool code itself runs in the eval's main process; only the work it requests through sandbox() runs in the container. The Sandboxing page says: 'There are two sandbox environments built in to Inspect and six available as external packages.' Its table (Environment Type / Package / Dockerfile-compatible / Description): docker (built-in, Yes, 'Docker local installation.'); k8s (inspect-k8s-sandbox, Yes, Kubernetes cluster); daytona (inspect-sandboxes, Yes, Daytona cloud sandbox); modal (inspect-sandboxes, Yes, Modal cloud sandbox); ec2 (inspect_ec2_sandbox, No, AWS EC2 virtual machine); proxmox (inspect_proxmox_sandbox, No, Proxmox VMs); vagrant (inspect_vagrant_sandbox, No, Vagrant VMs on any Vagrant-supported hypervisor); local (built-in, No, 'Local file system (no sandbox).'). The separate Extensions listing page additionally lists a Podman Sandbox (Vector Institute, inspect-podman) and a 'Policy Sandbox' (Arnab Mitra; 'Sandbox wrapper that allows fine grained control over command execution and file I/O'). E2B is NOT listed.
claims.quote: Model tool calls are executed within the main process running the evaluation task. However, the work that tools perform — such as running shell commands or executing Python code — very often needs to happen in a dedicated, isolated environment (for example, bash() runs its shell commands in a sandbox).
claims.location: Sandboxing > Overview; Sandboxing > Environment Binding (table); extensions/index > Sandboxes

claims.planned: SandboxEnvironment API: exec(cmd: list[str], input, cwd, env, user, timeout, …) → ExecResult(success, returncode, stdout, stderr); read_file / write_file; output limit (10 MiB?) and OutputLimitExceededError — verify exact current signature and limits
claims.finding: Signature today: async def exec(self, cmd: list[str], input: str | bytes | None = None, cwd: str | None = None, env: dict[str, str] = {}, user: str | None = None, timeout: int | None = None, timeout_retry: bool = True, concurrency: bool = True) -> ExecResult[str]. Documented raises: TimeoutError, UnicodeDecodeError, PermissionError. ExecResult is a dataclass with exactly four attributes: success (bool, 'Did the process exit with success'), returncode (int), stdout, stderr. Limits: exec output 10 MiB (source: 10 * 1024**2; docs say '10MB'), read_file 100 MiB (100 * 1024**2); both overridable with INSPECT_SANDBOX_MAX_EXEC_OUTPUT_SIZE / INSPECT_SANDBOX_MAX_READ_FILE_SIZE (bytes). CORRECTION to folklore: exec() overflow does NOT raise OutputLimitExceededError in the built-in providers — output is FRONT-TRUNCATED (only the trailing portion kept) and a successful ExecResult is returned, possibly silently incomplete. Only read_file() always raises OutputLimitExceededError. There is also a newer exec_remote() method (streaming/awaitable, with its own user option requiring the sandbox tools server to run as root), write_file(file, contents: str|bytes) which auto-creates parent dirs, read_file(file, text=True), and an optional connection() method.
claims.quote: read_file() always raises OutputLimitExceededError when the limit is exceeded. For exec() the behaviour depends on the sandbox provider: the built-in providers front-truncate each output stream (keeping only its trailing portion), so exec() returns a successful ExecResult whose stdout or stderr may be silently incomplete rather than raising.
claims.location: Sandboxing > Environment Interface > exec(); Sandboxing > Sandbox Limits; reference inspect_ai.util > ExecResult; source util/_sandbox/limits.py lines 8-9

claims.planned: Docker provider: with no compose file Inspect uses a default config (python image? `network_mode: none`? init: true? cpu/mem limits?) — get exact default compose YAML from the docs
claims.finding: The docs do not print the generated YAML, but state that with no config files Inspect 'Creates a sandbox environment based on the standard inspect-tool-support image' and that 'The generated Compose configuration sets network_mode: none'. The exact YAML is in the official source (COMPOSE_GENERIC_YAML, main branch, fetched 2026-09-20): services: default: image: "aisiuk/inspect-tool-support"; command: "tail -f /dev/null"; init: true; network_mode: none; stop_grace_period: 1s. With only a Dockerfile (COMPOSE_DOCKERFILE_YAML) it is the same but with build: {context: ".", dockerfile: "Dockerfile"} instead of image. CORRECTIONS: the default image is aisiuk/inspect-tool-support, not a plain python image; there are NO cpu or memory limits in the default config (the cpus: 1.0 / mem_limit: 0.5gb lines appear only in the docs' EXAMPLE compose file). CRITICAL CAVEAT: supplying your own compose file REPLACES the generated config, including network_mode: none — and Compose's own default is a network with outbound Internet access.
claims.quote: Supplying a custom Compose configuration — whether a Compose file or ComposeConfig — replaces the generated configuration rather than extending it, including its network_mode: none. Docker Compose's default is a project-scoped network with outbound Internet access, so include network_mode: none in your own configuration unless the evaluation requires networking.
claims.location: Sandboxing > Docker Configuration > Task Configuration; source src/inspect_ai/util/_sandbox/docker/config.py (COMPOSE_GENERIC_YAML, COMPOSE_DOCKERFILE_YAML)

claims.planned: Compose conventions: service named 'default' is the primary sandbox; `x-local`; images must keep running (command: tail -f /dev/null); per-sample compose projects; cleanup and `inspect sandbox cleanup docker`; --no-sandbox-cleanup for debugging and how to `docker exec` into it
claims.finding: Default-sandbox resolution order: (1) any service named 'default'; (2) any service with x-default: true; (3) the first service listed. x-local: true marks an image that is not on a remote registry and must not be pulled (tagged local images are also not pulled by default). 'init: true' lets the container respond to shutdown requests; 'command: tail -f /dev/null' stops the container exiting after start. Each sample gets its own sandbox instance even if the sandbox is defined at Task level. Cleanup is automatic; leftovers are removed with `inspect sandbox cleanup docker` (optionally + a container id). `--no-sandbox-cleanup` (or eval(..., sandbox_cleanup=False)) leaves containers up and prints their ids; shell in with `docker exec -it inspect-task-ielnkhh-default-1 bash -l`. Container names follow the pattern inspect-<task>-<random>-<service>-1. The docs do not use the phrase 'compose project per sample'; they say each sample gets its own sandbox instance.
claims.quote: (Note, each sample gets its own sandbox instance, even if the sandbox is defined at Task level. So samples do not interfere with each other's sandboxes.)
claims.location: Sandboxing > Per Sample Setup > Sandbox; > Multiple Environments; > Task Configuration; > Environment Cleanup

claims.planned: bash() tool: timeout param, user param; tool timeouts vs sample time_limit/working_limit; what the model sees on timeout
claims.finding: Signature: bash(timeout: int | None = None, user: str | None = None, sandbox: str | None = None, background: bool = False). timeout is in seconds and defaults to None (no timeout). user = 'User to execute commands as' (default: the sandbox's default user). The implementation runs sandbox.exec(cmd=["bash", "--login", "-c", command], timeout=timeout, user=user) and returns stderr followed by stdout as one string. Each call is a FRESH shell (no cwd/env carried over); multiple bash calls in one assistant message run concurrently (parallel=True). bash_session() is the stateful alternative (timeout default = wait_for_output + 5 s; wait_for_output default 30 s). python() has the same timeout/user/sandbox params. text_editor(timeout, user) defaults its timeout to 180 s. On timeout, sandbox().exec raises TimeoutError, which Inspect's default handling reports to the model as a tool error (the docs do not give the exact message text). Sample-level time_limit is wall-clock per sample; working_limit excludes time spent on rate-limit retries and waiting on shared resources (e.g. Docker containers or subprocess execution). Samples that hit limits are still scored. `background=True` is prompt-only: it only changes the tool description to suggest nohup … & and polling.
claims.quote: Note that we also set a timeout of 3 minutes for the bash() command. This isn't required but is often a good idea so that a single wayward bash command doesn't consume the entire time_limit.
claims.location: Setting Limits > Sample Limits > Time Limit / Working Limit; reference inspect_ai.tool > bash; Custom Tools > Tool Errors > Default Handling; source tool/_tools/_execute.py

claims.planned: Files/setup: Sample.files copied into sandbox, Sample.setup script; scorers can exec in the sandbox AFTER the agent is done (state-based grading) — and the integrity implication that anything in the sandbox was writable by the agent
claims.finding: Sample.files is a dict[str,str] (key = destination filename, optionally prefixed with a sandbox name e.g. "victim:flag.txt"; value = contents, a file path, or a base64 data URL). Sample.setup is a bash script executed in the default sandbox AFTER the files are copied. Scorers can call sandbox().read_file() or .exec() to inspect the sample's sandbox. PARTLY UNVERIFIABLE: the docs do NOT state the integrity implication (that the agent could have written anything the scorer reads) — that is the course's own inference, not an Inspect statement; present it as reasoning, not as a citation.
claims.quote: If your Solver is an Agent with tool use, you might want to inspect the contents of the tool sandbox to score the task. The contents of the sandbox for the Sample are available to the scorer; simply call await sandbox().read_file() (or .exec()).
claims.location: Multiple Scorers > Sandbox Access; Sandboxing > Per Sample Setup > Files / Script

claims.planned: Resource guidance: max_sandboxes default (2 * cpu count?), max_subprocesses, max_samples — verify
claims.finding: max_sandboxes: Docker provider default = 2 x the number of processors available to the eval (if the eval itself runs under a container CPU limit, that limit counts, not the host's cores). Applying max_sandboxes effectively caps max_samples at the same value. max_subprocesses default = number of processors available to the eval. max_samples default = max_connections + 1; max_connections default = 10 (so 11). Docs also advise: for > 30 concurrent containers, configure Docker's default address pools. Minimum versions: Docker Engine 24.0.6; Docker Compose 2.21.0 (2.22.0 when Inspect pulls images from a registry).
claims.quote: Individual sandbox providers can establish their own default limits (for example, the Docker provider defaults to twice the number of processors available to the eval — which under a container CPU limit such as docker --cpus or a Kubernetes limits.cpu is the limit rather than the host's processor count).
claims.location: Sandboxing > Resource Management > Max Sandboxes / Max Subprocesses / Max Samples; > Docker Configuration > Installation

claims.planned: Agent bridge / sandbox agent bridge: running external agents (Claude Code, Codex CLI) inside the sandbox with model calls proxied back to Inspect — what this means for network policy
claims.finding: sandbox_agent_bridge() runs a proxy server INSIDE the sandbox container on localhost port 13131 (agent configured with e.g. OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:13131/v1, ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:13131, GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:13131/v1beta). The proxy relays requests to the current Inspect model provider (outside the container), so the CLI agent needs no direct internet route for model calls. It listens only on the sandbox's loopback. Network-policy consequence the docs spell out: provider-side tools (web_search, web_fetch, code_execution, remote MCP servers) execute OUTSIDE the sandbox at the model provider, so they would bypass the sandbox's egress policy; the bridge therefore withholds them unless the eval explicitly grants them (e.g. sandbox_agent_bridge(state, web_search=True)). Media in requests must be inline data: URIs for the same reason. Claude Code, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI are named; ready-made agents live in the separate 'Inspect SWE' package (meridianlabs-ai/inspect_swe).
claims.quote: Some tools a bridged agent can request are executed outside the sandbox — web_search, web_fetch, code_execution, and remote MCP servers all run at the model provider. An agent that names one of these in a request therefore reaches the network regardless of the sandbox's own egress policy, so sandbox_agent_bridge() withholds them unless the evaluation grants them
claims.location: Agent Bridge > Sandbox Bridge; Agent Bridge > (provider-side tools paragraph after the Sandbox Bridge example)

extra_findings: network_mode: none only restricts processes INSIDE the container; tool/scorer code and the model provider run outside it. Quote: 'The network_mode: none entry applies only to processes inside the container. It does not restrict network access from the evaluation process or model provider. Code in custom tools, agents or scorers may therefore access the internet outside the Docker sandbox. Tools that do not use the Inspect sandbox, such as web_search(), are also unaffected.' (Sandboxing > Docker Configuration > Task Configuration)

How to give a sandbox network access correctly. Quote: 'If the evaluation does need network access, omit network_mode — that provides outbound access while keeping the project's network isolated (network_mode: bridge would instead join Docker's shared built-in bridge, so prefer omitting it). When services only need to communicate with each other, use an internal network, which allows service-to-service traffic without external connectivity.' (Sandboxing > Task Configuration)

The docs' canonical example compose.yaml (an EXAMPLE, not the default): services: default: build: . / init: true / command: tail -f /dev/null / cpus: 1.0 / mem_limit: 0.5gb / network_mode: none. Quote: 'The init: true entry enables the container to respond to shutdown requests. The command is provided to prevent the container from exiting after it starts.' (Sandboxing > Task Configuration)

Config-file discovery table: no files -> 'Creates a sandbox environment based on the standard inspect-tool-support image'; Dockerfile -> 'Creates a sandbox environment by building the image'; compose.yaml -> 'Creates sandbox environment(s) based on compose.yaml'. 'By default, any Dockerfile and/or compose.yaml file within the task directory will be automatically discovered and used.' Alternate file: sandbox=("docker", "attacker-compose.yaml"). (Sandboxing > Environment Binding / Task Configuration)

The 'local' sandbox is no sandbox. Quote (extension docs): 'local — Run sandbox() methods in the same file system as the running evaluation (should only be used if you are already running your evaluation in another sandbox).' (Extensions > Sandboxes, intro table)

Why output limits exist. Quote: 'By default, sandboxes limit the size of file reads to 100MB and execution output to 10MB. These limits exist to prevent boundary cases of outputs or executions that don't terminate and result in OOM or hung evaluations (i.e. they usually indicate an error by the model).' And the practical advice: 'If a command can produce output near the limit and you need all of it, have the command write to a file and read it with read_file().' (Sandboxing > Sandbox Limits)

timeout_retry: exec() retries timed-out commands by default. Quote: 'the exec() method includes a timeout_retry parameter that defaults to True... No more than 2 retries should be attempted and both with timeouts less than 60 seconds. If you are executing commands that are not idempotent ... then you can specify timeout_retry=False'. (Sandboxing > exec())

Expected vs unexpected errors. Expected errors (TimeoutError, PermissionError, UnicodeDecodeError, OutputLimitExceededError, ToolError) 'will be handled and reported to the model'; 'Unexpected errors (e.g. a network error communicating with a remote service or container runtime) on the other hand are not automatically handled and result in the Sample failing with an error.' This is Inspect's built-in separation of 'model failed' from 'infrastructure failed'. (Custom Tools > Tool Errors > Default Handling)

Sample limits do not error the sample. Quote: 'Sample limits don't result in errors, but rather an early exit from execution (samples that encounter limits are still scored, albeit nearly always as "incorrect").' (Setting Limits > Sample Limits)

working_limit definition. Quote: 'Working time is computed based on total clock time minus time spent on (a) unsuccessful model generations (e.g. rate limited requests); and (b) waiting on shared resources (e.g. Docker containers or subprocess execution).' (Setting Limits > Working Limit)

bash() statelessness. Quote: 'Each call spawns a fresh subprocess and holds no per-call state, so multiple bash tool calls in the same assistant message run concurrently. The model is responsible for sequencing commands that depend on each other's filesystem side effects.' And: 'a detached process keeps running between bash() calls even though each call executes in a fresh shell.' (reference inspect_ai.tool > bash; Standard Tools > Background Tasks)

bash_session(). Quote: 'provides a bash shell that retains its state across calls from the model (as distinct from the bash() tool which executes each command in a fresh session). The prompt, working directory, and environment variables are all retained across calls.' Signature: bash_session(*, timeout=None  # default is max_wait + 5 seconds, wait_for_output=None  # default is 30 seconds, user=None, instance=None). (Standard Tools > Bash Session; reference)

Multiple services / infrastructure: a compose file may define extra hosts (e.g. 'victim') addressed as sandbox("victim"), shared named volumes, and Sample metadata is interpolated into compose files as SAMPLE_METADATA_<KEY> env vars, e.g. mem_limit: ${SAMPLE_METADATA_MEMORY_LIMIT-0.5gb} (the '-default' suffix is needed because the file is also read without a sample when images are built). (Sandboxing > Multiple Environments / Infrastructure / Sample Metadata)

--sandbox-prebuilt (or INSPECT_EVAL_SANDBOX_PREBUILT) skips image builds and verifies images exist locally, for air-gapped machines; 'A missing image results in an error before any samples run.' (Sandboxing > Prebuilt Images)

Sandbox provider lifecycle hooks: task_init (once per unique config — pull/build images), sample_init (create environments per Sample), sample_cleanup, task_cleanup, cli_cleanup (backs `inspect sandbox cleanup`). (Extensions > Sandboxes > Lifecycle Methods)

Human baselining uses the same box: 'Human agents are just a special type of agent that use the identical dataset, sandbox, and scorer configuration that models use', logging in with e.g. `docker exec -it inspect-gdm_intercod-itmzq4e-default-1 bash -l`. (Human Agent)

Troubleshooting: 'Trace logs record the beginning and end of calls to subprocess() (e.g. tool calls that run commands in sandboxes) as well as control commands sent to Docker Compose. The inspect trace anomalies subcommand then enables you to query for commands that don't terminate, timeout, or have errors.' (Sandboxing > Troubleshooting)

Programmatic config: ComposeConfig / ComposeService (from inspect_ai.util) mirror compose files (image, build, command, environment, volumes, ports, mem_limit, cpus, network_mode, x- extension fields) and are passed as SandboxEnvironmentSpec("docker", config). (Sandboxing > Programmatic Configuration)
teaching_notes: Three corrections to folklore that matter for pages 25-28: (1) exec() output over 10 MiB is silently FRONT-truncated by the built-in providers, not an exception — a scorer parsing JSON from stdout can be silently wrong; (2) the default sandbox image is aisiuk/inspect-tool-support with network_mode: none, init: true, stop_grace_period: 1s and NO cpu/memory limits; (3) the moment you supply your own compose.yaml you LOSE network_mode: none unless you write it yourself — Compose's default network has outbound internet. Also: network_mode: none says nothing about what tool/scorer code on the host can reach, and the agent-bridge docs explicitly note that provider-side tools (web_search etc.) bypass sandbox egress policy. The docs never say 'anything a scorer reads from the sandbox was writable by the agent' — that is our inference; the docs only confirm scorers can read_file()/exec() in the sample's sandbox. The default YAML is quoted from the official source file because the docs page only describes it.
